analysis.one_liner: Lets churches and tax-exempt groups endorse and campaign for candidates while keeping tax exemption.
analysis.headline: Introduced on the first day of the 115th Congress with 5 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the same day and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1954, the tax code has barred churches and other tax-exempt organizations from backing or opposing candidates for office. This bill strikes that ban. Congregations and their pastors could then endorse and campaign for candidates while keeping their tax exemption, and donations to them would remain tax-deductible. The bill leaves federal campaign finance law unchanged, so churches could not donate directly to campaigns, but the ban on campaign activity inside tax-exempt institutions would be gone.
analysis.who_benefits: Churches and other 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organizations, and their clergy, who want to endorse and oppose candidates without risking their tax status. Political campaigns and party organizations also benefit, because tax-exempt institutions would become willing, subsidized channels of campaign activity: donations to churches and nonprofits are tax-deductible, so money routed into electioneering through them would effectively be partly paid for by other taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deletes the provision of section 501(c) of the Internal Revenue Code that bars tax-exempt organizations from participating in or intervening in political campaigns on behalf of or in opposition to candidates, which has applied since 1954.

It applies to taxable years ending after enactment, and it expressly does not invalidate or limit the Federal Election Campaign Act, meaning churches could still not make direct campaign contributions under existing campaign finance law.
Supporters frame the change as restoring the First Amendment rights of churches, which currently must give up or risk their tax exemption to speak about candidates.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and voters. Donations to churches and tax-exempt groups are tax-deductible, so political campaigning funded through those donations would be partly subsidized by everyone else's taxes. The change would also open a new route for election money through institutions that do not publicly report their politics, at a cost to transparency for ordinary voters.

drawbacks.text: The repeal is not limited to houses of worship: it removes the campaign ban for every type of 501(c)(3) exempt organization, including charities and foundations, so nonprofit money that donors expect to go to charitable work could be steered into elections.

Because donations to these organizations are tax-deductible, election spending channeled through them would be partially paid for by other taxpayers, and the organizations would not have to disclose their political activity the way campaigns and traditional political groups do.

The bill leaves the Federal Election Campaign Act unchanged, so the new campaign freedom for tax-exempt groups would operate outside the contribution limits and reporting rules that apply to political committees, a gap an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine free-speech case here: the 1954 rule restricts what pastors and religious leaders can say about candidates, and some congregations see that as a government speech restriction. But the remedy is broad and blunt. It removes the campaign ban for all tax-exempt organizations, not just churches, and it turns the tax deduction into a partial public subsidy for election spending that voters cannot trace. The narrow free-speech benefit comes bundled with a significant cost to campaign transparency.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing or a vote; it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Walter B. Jones of North Carolina introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over the tax code.
Five Republican members cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a hearing or marked up the bill, and it never reached the House floor for a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the current rules stayed in place: tax-exempt organizations still cannot campaign for candidates, and tax-deductible giving still cannot be routed into electioneering. Taxpayers and voters who rely on campaign-finance transparency came out ahead, while churches that wanted the freedom to endorse candidates got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Walter B. Jones
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 3, 2017 to repeal the 1954 Johnson Amendment.

for.name: 5 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats signed on.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill; it sat in committee for the full two-year Congress without advancing.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 5 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors, and the bill never reached a vote where party splits could be measured.

industries.note: Repeal would let congregations and clergy endorse and oppose candidates while keeping their tax exemption, and donations financing that activity would remain tax-deductible, meaning other taxpayers partially subsidize it. The gain is political power for institutions at the cost of transparency for voters.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt charities and foundations (501(c)(3) sector generally)
industries.note: The bill removes the campaign ban for all 501(c)(3) organizations, not just churches, giving charities new political speech rights. But it also means donor money intended for charitable work could be redirected into elections, which many in the charitable sector see as a cost to their mission.

Tax-exempt institutions would become available as channels for campaign activity, since the bill keeps campaign finance law unchanged and these groups are not required to report political spending the way political committees do. That expands the pool of election money that voters cannot trace.
